intro: Schubert’s Unfinished begins with cellos and basses alone, then oboe and clarinet play the melody over the violins. Leopold Stokowski conducts the Philadelphia Orchestra in this 1927 recording of the first movement.

sections.label: A · Low strings, then two woodwinds
sections.mNote: B minor, then the cellos’ melody in G major

sections.label: Dev · Low-string opening theme in E minor
sections.mNote: The opening phrase rises to a climax led by trombones

sections.label: A′ · Oboe and clarinet return
sections.mNote: The violin murmur returns beneath the oboe and clarinet.

sections.label: Coda · Low strings, B minor
sections.mNote: The opening phrase returns and leads to the final chords.

cues.title: Cellos and basses alone
cues.text: The symphony opens with eight bars for cellos and basses, pianissimo, playing a phrase in B minor. The violins then enter, and oboe and clarinet play together above them.
cues.evidence: Schubert’s Werke, Series I, No. 8 (Breitkopf & Härtel, 1885), first movement, pp. 1–2. The opening and scoring are also described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The score in Graz, 1865
cues.text: Schubert’s fair copy of these two movements passed to the brothers Josef and Anselm Hüttenbrenner. In 1860 Josef told the conductor Johann Herbeck that Anselm owned a “treasure”. Herbeck called on Anselm in Graz in May 1865, and an overture by Anselm shared the première programme.
cues.evidence: Josef Hüttenbrenner to Herbeck, 8 March 1860, quoted by Phillip Huscher (Chicago Symphony Orchestra, 2021) and Herbert Glass (Los Angeles Philharmonic): Anselm “possesses a treasure in Schubert’s B Minor symphony”. Benjamin-Gunnar Cohrs, “Schuberts Unvollendete: Eine Bestandsaufnahme” (2008), citing the Schubert-Lexikon: the score reached Anselm in Graz from Josef at an unknown date, Herbeck visited Anselm on 1 May 1865, and the charge that Anselm withheld the score is probably unjust. Glass and Wolfgang Stähr (Berliner Philharmoniker): an overture by Anselm on the programme of 17 December 1865. https://www.chicagosymphony.org/inside-the-music/article/7349/the-mystery-of-schuberts-unfinished-symphony https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-8-unfinished https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/884.html https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/programme-notes/franz-schubert-symphony-no-7-in-b-minor-d-759-unfinished

cues.title: Second subject, cellos, G major
cues.text: After a short bridge led by the horns, the cellos begin a long melody in G major. The violins take it up over a syncopated accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1885), first movement, bars 38–41 and the following second subject; melody, key and syncopated accompaniment described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Tutti chords in the closing group
cues.text: Heavy chords from the full orchestra interrupt the melody in G major. Schubert leaves silences between the chords. Fragments of the tune then pass through the closing passage.
cues.evidence: First movement, exposition closing group: tutti sforzandi, pauses and variants of the G-major theme. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Symphony set aside, 1822
cues.text: Schubert set the symphony aside in 1822 for a commissioned piece and never returned to it. The reason is unknown. One theory holds that he found no finale to match the opening; others cite illness, lack of time and no prospect of a performance.
cues.evidence: Wolfgang Stähr, Berliner Philharmoniker programme note on Symphony No. 7 (8) in B minor, D 759, first paragraph. https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/programme-notes/franz-schubert-symphony-no-7-in-b-minor-d-759-unfinished

cues.title: Development in E minor
cues.text: The development begins in E minor with the phrase that opened the symphony. The low strings play it first, and the higher strings take it up.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1885), first movement, p. 7; the E-minor development of the introductory theme is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Development climax, trombones
cues.text: At the climax of the development the trombones play a variant of the opening phrase, first heard in the lowest strings, above the orchestra. The music stays in E minor through the long climax.
cues.evidence: First movement, development climax: prominent trombone variant of the introductory theme in E minor. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Vienna, 1865
cues.text: On 17 December 1865 Johann von Herbeck conducted the first performance in Vienna, forty-three years after Schubert began the score. He followed its two completed movements with the finale of Schubert’s Third Symphony.
cues.evidence: Benjamin-Gunnar Cohrs, “Schuberts Unvollendete: Eine Bestandsaufnahme” (2008): Herbeck conducts the first performance on 17 December 1865 and takes the finale of the Third Symphony as an emergency finale. Wolfgang Stähr, Berliner Philharmoniker programme note: the première in 1865, forty-three years after the symphony’s creation. Phillip Huscher, Chicago Symphony Orchestra (2021): the Third Symphony’s finale tacked on. https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/884.html https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/programme-notes/franz-schubert-symphony-no-7-in-b-minor-d-759-unfinished https://chicagosymphony.org/inside-the-music/article/7349/the-mystery-of-schuberts-unfinished-symphony

cues.title: Recapitulation, oboe and clarinet
cues.text: Oboe and clarinet return over the violins after the trombones. Schubert brings back their melody in B minor and leaves out the eight-bar introduction.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1885), first movement, pp. 11–12: end of development and recapitulation. https://imslp.org/wiki/Symphony_No.8,_D.759_(Schubert,_Franz)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second subject, recapitulation
cues.text: In the recapitulation the cello melody returns in D major, a fourth below its first appearance in G major.
cues.evidence: First movement, second subject in the recapitulation, transposed from G major to D major. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Stokowski’s second recording, 1927
cues.text: Stokowski and the Philadelphians recorded this symphony acoustically in 1924. They recorded it again in April 1927 using the electrical process, which, in Pristine’s words, conveys “the burnished sheen of the strings” in a swiftly flowing reading.
cues.evidence: Mark Obert-Thorn’s producer’s note, Pristine Classical PASC 483: a return to the 1924 acoustic recording (PASC 441) in April 1927. https://www.pristineclassical.com/products/pasc483

cues.title: Coda in B minor
cues.text: The recapitulation closes in B major. The coda returns to B minor and is built on the introductory theme, first heard in the low strings, and the movement ends with loud chords for the full orchestra.
cues.evidence: First movement, B-major close of the recapitulation and B-minor coda based on the introductory theme. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Opening bass phrase, third appearance
cues.text: Wolfgang Stähr wrote that on its third appearance the basses’ opening phrase sinks into the abyss and sets off howling and groaning, “as if graves were opening”.
cues.evidence: Wolfgang Stähr, Berliner Philharmoniker programme note on Symphony No. 7 (8) in B minor, D 759, on the third appearance of the basses’ opening phrase. https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/programme-notes/franz-schubert-symphony-no-7-in-b-minor-d-759-unfinished
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A B pedal, then E minor
transitions.from: A · Low strings, then two woodwinds
transitions.to: Dev · Low-string opening theme in E minor
transitions.how: The exposition ends with B held in the second bassoon and first horn beneath an F♯-major chord. The development then begins softly in E minor. Cellos and basses play the opening phrase again, and the higher strings take it up.
transitions.evidence: First movement, bar 109 and the opening of the development; Breitkopf & Härtel score (1885), p. 7. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert)

transitions.title: The violin murmur returns
transitions.from: Dev · Low-string opening theme in E minor
transitions.how: The orchestral outburst dies away into soft phrases for flute and oboe. Oboe and clarinet then play the B-minor melody again over murmuring violins and plucked lower strings. The eight-bar introduction is omitted.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1885), first movement, pp. 11–12. https://imslp.org/wiki/Symphony_No.8,_D.759_(Schubert,_Franz)

transitions.title: B major to B minor at the coda
transitions.how: The recapitulation closes in B major. At the coda the key changes to B minor, and the opening phrase returns in the low strings. From there the coda builds to the orchestra’s closing chords.
transitions.evidence: First movement, end of recapitulation and coda. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert)

source.title: Schubert, Symphonie in H moll (unvollendet), Schubert’s Werke, Serie 1 Nr. 8 (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, 1885)
source.locator: IMSLP #73284, first movement, Allegro moderato, printed pages 1–18.

timeline.note: Cellos and basses begin alone, pianissimo, in B minor.
Violins play above plucked violas, cellos and basses.
Oboe and clarinet play in unison over the violins.
Four bars of horns and bassoons prepare G major.
Cellos, then violins, play the G-major tune over off-beat strings.
The full orchestra plays sforzando chords, with silences between them.
Cellos and basses play the opening phrase again, quietly, in E minor; the upper strings take it up.
Trombones play the opening phrase over the full orchestra.
Flutes and oboes play the quiet phrases that close the development.
Oboe and clarinet return above the violins’ B-minor figure.
The low strings play the opening phrase again as the coda begins.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The performing edition and any cuts or retouchings by the conductor are not identified in the sources consulted.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Bolig dates all three sides of the first movement (CVE-29052, -29053 and -29054) to 28 April 1927. The Internet Archive description and Pristine give the two session days (28 and 30 April 1927) for the symphony as a whole.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Academy of Music, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Stokowski’s earlier acoustic recording of 1924 used the same matrix numbers without the CVE prefix and different issue numbers (Bolig lists 74894–74897 and 6459–6460); this transfer is the electrical recording of 1927 by its description, session dates and Victor numbers.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The Internet Archive description says “Originally issued as Victor 6663, 6664 & 6665. (Later as a set as M-16.)”; Pristine gives the same numbers and album. Bolig also lists later Victor and HMV issues of the same sides. The disc and side on which the movement boundary falls are not identified; the allocation of matrices to movements follows Bolig’s part numbers.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Parts 1–3: CVE-29052, take 6; CVE-29053, take 6; CVE-29054, take 6
fields.note: Bolig and the Pristine producer’s note agree on the matrices and takes of the first movement. The DAHR matrix pages could not be opened on 17 October 2026 (503 error). No run-out inspection has been made of the digital surrogate.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The Internet Archive description reads “Transfer by Bob Varney”.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is identified. The Internet Archive item was added on 24 January 2011, which is an upload date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: The stylus, equalisation, speed and noise treatment are not documented. The file runs 10:28; Pristine’s own restoration runs 10:33, so the two transfers differ by a few seconds, and where the side joins fall in this file is not known.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Schubert died in 1828. This is a term calculation, not a worldwide clearance or a statement about an unidentified modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis).
fields.note: The Internet Archive item carries a CC0 licence URL declared by the uploader, which is not treated as authority to waive Victor’s rights. The pre-1963 European rule applies because the recording was made in 1927 and was on sale by January 1928 (a Victor advertisement in The Golden Book Magazine offers Records Nos. 6663-4-5), so the 50-year term expired before the 2013 extension; the exact first issue date is not established. This is territorial, not a worldwide licence. The recording was published after 1925, so a US public-domain basis is not established.
alts: Pre-1963 European public domain — territorial basis.
CC0 — licence URL on the Internet Archive item, uploader’s declaration.

composer.epithet: Composer who at seventeen wrote a song for Gretchen with a spinning-wheel accompaniment and at thirty-one wrote music for two cellos.
facts: Vienna Stadtkonvikt, 1808–13; composition lessons with Antonio Salieri
School assistant; tutor to the Esterházy daughters at Zseliz in 1818 and 1824; independent composer
The singer Vogl, the poets Schober and Mayrhofer, the painter Schwind, Josef von Spaun
More than 600 songs; symphonies, chamber music, piano sonatas and duets, masses and stage works

quote.text: I like these songs more than all the others, and you will come to like them too.
quote.source: Schubert to his friends about Winterreise, 1827, as Josef von Spaun later recalled; our translation

composer.background:
In the Schubert family quartet, Franz played the viola, his brothers the violins and his father the cello. He was born on 31 January 1797 in Himmelpfortgrund, a Viennese suburb, and grew up in his father’s schoolhouse. His father taught him violin, his brother Ignaz piano, and the parish musician Michael Holzer taught him further. At eleven he entered the imperial chapel choir and the Stadtkonvikt boarding school, where he played Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven in the school orchestra.

Salieri began teaching him composition in 1812. The next year Schubert left the boarding school, trained as a teacher and returned to his father’s classroom as an assistant. On 19 October 1814, aged seventeen, he wrote Gretchen am Spinnrade. In the piano part the right hand imitates the spinning wheel and the left hand the treadle, while Goethe’s Gretchen sings of her thoughts of Faust. At the point where she recalls his kiss, the accompaniment figure stops. The following year brought roughly 140 songs, among them Erlkönig, as well as church music, a symphony and works for the stage.
